column2: Put a book flat on a table. Tip its far edge up, a quarter turn. Then roll it a quarter turn to the right. Now start over, and swap the order. Roll first, then tip. Does the book end up the same way?
No. Tip first, and the cover ends up facing you. Roll first, and it faces the wall on your right.
Sliding is nothing like this. Slide the book right, then away, or away, then right, and it lands on the same spot. Positions add. Orientations don't.
This is a KUKA robot arm with seven joints. Its job is to put its gripper at a pose, a position and an orientation together.
So its software must do arithmetic with things that refuse to add. The way out is about a hundred and fifty years old, and by the end you'll read it in one line.
Look where tip then roll left the book. It could have got there in a single turn, about a single axis.
Two quarter turns went in. How big is that single turn?
A third of a turn. A hundred and twenty degrees, about the diagonal through the book's corner.
That always works. Any turn followed by any turn is one turn about one axis. Euler showed it in seventeen seventy-five.
And any turn can be undone. A collection where you can combine any two, and undo any one, is called a group.
To compute, track where the book's three edges point. Three arrows, three numbers each. Nine numbers in a grid, a matrix. One turn after another is one matrix times another.
Nine numbers is a lot for one orientation. Three should do. Here is a machine that tries, a gimbal. Three rings, one inside the next, each turning about its own axis.
Turn the middle ring a quarter turn. Now the outer ring's axis and the inner ring's axis line up. Do those two rings still do different things?
No. They turn the book about the very same axis. Three rings, but only two ways to turn. This is gimbal lock.
It happened on the way to the Moon. Apollo steered by three gimbals. Past seventy degrees on the middle one, a warning lamp lit. Past eighty-five, the computer gave up its reference.
On Apollo eleven, Michael Collins radioed a request. How about sending me a fourth gimbal for Christmas.
It wasn't bad engineering. Any way of naming every orientation with just three numbers has a bad spot somewhere.
Angles hide a second trap. Two compass headings. One is a hundred and seventy degrees. The other is minus a hundred and seventy.
What heading is halfway between them?
Average the numbers and you get zero. Straight ahead. But both arrows point almost straight back. The honest halfway is a hundred and eighty, the exact opposite.

But zoom in on one point of the circle. Up close, it looks straight. So measure from one heading to the other as a turn. Twenty degrees. Take half. Ten degrees on from the first is a hundred and eighty.
That is the whole trick, and the rest of this video is that trick again and again. The space is curved. Do the arithmetic on the flat piece that touches it. Then roll the answer back on.
For orientations, the flat piece is made of spins. Start from doing nothing, and begin to turn. Say which axis, and how fast. That is one arrow, along the axis, as long as the speed.
Arrows are easy. They add, they stretch, they average, with no bad spots.
Hold one spin steady for one second, and the book ends at some orientation. That step, from a spin to an orientation, is called the exponential.
Spin the book about the diagonal through its corner, at a third of a turn per second. After one second, where do its three edges point?
Each edge lands where the next one was. That is where the book ended in the first quiz, with roll first.
There is a formula for this step. Split any point into the part along the axis, which stays, and the part going around, which swings on a circle. It is called Rodrigues' formula.
A smooth space of motions like this, where you can combine and undo, is a Lie group, after the Norwegian mathematician Sophus Lie. Its flat piece is its Lie algebra.

Poses work the same way. Start on a floor. This is a KUKA mobile base. Its wheels carry slanted rollers, so it can drive forward, slide sideways and spin, all at once. Its pose is three numbers. So is its velocity.
Hold one velocity for six seconds. Forward at half a meter per second, spinning at thirty degrees per second. Where does the base end up?
Beside where it started. Just under two meters to its left, facing backward. It drove a half circle.
Add six seconds of velocity onto the pose, and you predict three meters straight ahead. The exponential gets it right. A steady velocity carries the base around a fixed point.
On a floor, that is every steady motion there is. A turn about some point. Or, with no spin, a straight slide.
Now leave the floor. In space, a velocity is two arrows. A spin, and a slide. Six numbers, which roboticists call a twist.
Hold a twist steady, and you get the motion of a screw. The body turns about an axis, and slides along that same axis.
A door is a screw with no slide. A drawer is a screw with no turn. A bottle cap does both.
Here is the surprise. Pick up the book. Put it down anywhere, facing any way. One screw would have carried it there. Every time.
Michel Chasles published that in eighteen thirty. Giulio Mozzi had found the axis in seventeen sixty-three.
So how many numbers does a pose in space need?
Six. Three for position, three for orientation. Yet software stores nine numbers for an orientation, or four. The spare ones are the price of having no bad spots.
Back to the arm. Standing straight up, it is one point three meters tall. Each of its seven joints is a hinge. A hinge does one thing. It turns about its own axis.
A turn about an axis is a screw with no slide. So the arm is seven screws, stacked.
Suppose only joint four turns, the elbow. Which parts of the arm move?
Everything past the elbow, as one rigid piece. Nothing before it. Each joint applies its screw to everything further out.
That gives a recipe. Start with the gripper's pose when every joint is at zero. Apply the last joint's screw, then the one before, down to the first.
Each screw, held for its joint angle, is an exponential. So the gripper's pose is a product of seven exponentials, the line from the start. Roger Brockett presented it in nineteen eighty-three.
Try it by hand, with the real arm's lengths.
Bend two joints a quarter turn each, the shoulder and the elbow. The recipe says, elbow first. With the arm still straight up, the elbow's screw swings the forearm over until it lies level.
Then the shoulder's screw swings everything, about the shoulder's axis, just where it stood at zero. The upper arm comes down level, and the forearm points straight up.
Notice what the recipe never asked. Where the elbow's axis is now. Each screw is written down once, with the arm at zero.
Now joint one, at the base, turns a quarter turn about the vertical. Where does the gripper go?
Round to the side, at the same height. It was forty-two centimeters in front of the base. Now it is forty-two centimeters to the side.
Now speeds. If the joints are turning, how is the gripper moving?
Each joint, turning alone, moves the gripper along that joint's screw. That is a twist. And twists live on the flat piece, so they add.
Seven joints, seven twists, six numbers each. Stand them side by side. A grid, six rows by seven columns, called the Jacobian. Joint speeds go in. The gripper's twist comes out.
The arm is in an L shape. Which joint moves the gripper's tip fastest, at the same turning speed? Joint one, two or seven?

Joint two. What counts is how far the tip is from each axis. Sixty-seven centimeters from the shoulder's. Forty-two from the base's. And the tip sits right on joint seven's axis, so that joint only spins it.
And the columns change as the arm moves, because its axes move with it.
Six rows means six independent directions for the gripper to move in. Usually, seven joints cover all six.
Here the arm is stretched straight out. Can the gripper still move in all six directions?
No. It can't move further out, and it can't even begin to pull straight back. Along the arm, every joint's push is zero. Four of the six directions are left.
A pose like this is called a singularity. Close to one, small motions of the gripper cost huge joint speeds.

Pull the gripper straight back at ten centimeters per second. With the elbow bent thirty degrees, it must turn at fifty-four degrees per second. Bent ten degrees, a hundred and sixty. Its limit is seventy-five.
You have met this before. The wrist is three joints whose axes meet at one point. A gimbal. Straighten it, and two of its axes line up, exactly like the rings.
Seven joints. Six numbers in a pose. One joint is spare. What does it buy?
Try it on yourself. Lay your palm flat on a desk and keep your shoulder still. Can your elbow still move?
It can. It swings on an arc while your hand stays put. Counted the way a roboticist counts, your arm has seven joints too.
The robot does the same. Its gripper holds one pose, while its elbow swings on a circle twenty-nine centimeters in radius.
In the Jacobian, that is a set of joint speeds whose twists add up to nothing.
Now the question a robot really faces. Here is the pose I want. Which joint angles get me there?
There is rarely a tidy formula, so the arm takes steps. First, compare the pose it has with the pose it wants. One screw joins them. Read as a twist, that screw is the error.
Second, ask the Jacobian which joint speeds make that twist, and move the joints that way. Third, look again, and repeat.
The gripper starts half a meter from its goal, and a quarter turn off. How many steps until it is within a tenth of a millimeter?
Three. Half a meter off. Then nine centimeters. Then four millimeters. Then three hundredths of a millimeter. It is Newton's method, running on a curved space.
Why not just subtract angles? Because of the two traps. These two orientations are one point four degrees apart. Yet two of their three angles differ by ninety.
One more question. Between the start and the goal, what should the gripper do on the way?
Blend the two orientations, number by number. Half of one matrix plus half of the other. Is the result halfway there?
It is not even an orientation. A gripper turned by that blend would be squashed to half its volume. A blend of two different turns is never a turn.
The honest path is the screw. Take the twist that joins the two poses, and hold it for half a second. Half the turn and half the slide, and every pose on the way is a true pose.
Real robots often let the tip travel a straight line instead. Here the screw bows away from that line by seven point six centimeters.

The same moves run far beyond this arm. Drones steer poses. Mapping robots average them. A humanoid's whole body floats, so its state is one free pose, plus the angle of every joint. For this one, twenty-nine.

And a physics engine steps every body forward by a small twist. How it steps matters. Add the spin onto the nine numbers a thousand times, and the body has swollen by ten percent. With the exponential, it stays rigid.
Last one. Tip the book one degree, then roll it one degree. Then the other order. Do the two results still differ?
They do, by less than two hundredths of a degree. And that leftover is itself a turn, about the one axis neither turn used.
For quarter turns the leftover was a third of a turn. For small turns it shrinks like the product of the two angles. That is the Lie bracket. It measures how much order matters.
So the arm does not add orientations. It multiplies motions, and does its adding on the flat piece. That is what it means to think in Lie groups.
